title: Pydantic: validate real data
summary: Twenty practical lessons using Pydantic 2: models, constraints, validators, nested data, unions, serialization and JSON Schema. Every example runs independently.

lessons.title: Parse a boundary with BaseModel
lessons.body:
# Parse a boundary with BaseModel

Type hints describe a Python function, but they do not validate a dictionary received from JSON. A Pydantic model turns that boundary into executable rules. Constructing the model converts supported input values and rejects values that cannot satisfy the field types.

The result is a model instance with typed attributes. Use `model_dump()` to produce a dictionary for the next layer. Keep the original input available when diagnosing bad data; validation should not mutate the caller's dictionary.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Count(BaseModel):
    value: int

item = Count(value="12")
print(item.value, type(item.value).__name__)
print(item.model_dump())
```
lessons.task: Define User with integer id and string name. Implement load_user(raw) returning its validated dictionary. Accept integer strings for id, ignore unknown fields, and reject missing or invalid fields.

checks.name: rejects invalid input
ignores extras without mutation

hints: Declare id as int and name as str on a BaseModel.
Validate raw with model_validate, then return model_dump so extras are not copied into the output.

BaseModel performs parsing at construction. model_validate accepts the incoming object, while model_dump returns only the declared fields. A successful type hint alone would not provide these guarantees.
lessons.explanation: BaseModel performs parsing at construction. model_validate accepts the incoming object, while model_dump returns only the declared fields. A successful type hint alone would not provide these guarantees.

lessons.title: Choose strict validation deliberately
lessons.body:
# Choose strict validation deliberately

Automatic conversion is useful at a text boundary, but it can hide a mistake inside an already typed system. Strict fields require the expected Python type instead of accepting every convertible value. In particular, a boolean should not silently become a measurement just because Python treats bool as a subclass of int.

Pydantic offers strictness per model, per field and per validation call. Choose the boundary that owns the policy. A strict model makes the rule visible to every caller.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
from pydantic import ValidationError
class Sample(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)
    count: int
try:
    Sample(count="3")
except ValidationError as error:
    print(error.errors()[0]["type"])
```
lessons.task: Define strict Measurement with count: int. Implement strict_count(raw) returning its count. Reject numeric strings, bools and floats; accept zero and negative integers.

checks.name: rejects coercion

hints: Set model_config to ConfigDict(strict=True) on Measurement.
Return the validated count; numeric strings, floats and bools must fail before you return it.
ConfigDict(strict=True) is attached to the model, so all of its fields share the same conversion policy. Range validation is a separate decision from type strictness.
lessons.explanation: ConfigDict(strict=True) is attached to the model, so all of its fields share the same conversion policy. Range validation is a separate decision from type strictness.

lessons.title: Constrain fields with Field
lessons.body:
# Constrain fields with Field

A valid Python type can still carry an invalid domain value. A negative quantity is an integer, and an empty label is a string. Field constraints combine those domain rules with the type so every construction path checks the same conditions.

Use inclusive and exclusive bounds carefully: `ge` includes its boundary, while `gt` excludes it. String length is checked on the value you actually validate. If whitespace should be removed first, add an explicit normalization rule rather than assuming length validation strips it.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
class Page(BaseModel):
    size: int = Field(ge=1, le=50)
print(Page(size=10).model_dump())
```
lessons.task: Define Product with name length 1..40, price greater than zero, and stock integer at least zero. product_data(raw) returns its validated dictionary.

checks.name: checks numeric bounds
checks name bounds

hints: Put min_length/max_length on name, gt on price and ge on stock.
Zero stock is allowed, but zero price and an empty name are not.
Field keeps range and length rules next to their fields. Pydantic reports the field that failed, so callers do not have to infer which condition a hand-written boolean represented.
lessons.explanation: Field keeps range and length rules next to their fields. Pydantic reports the field that failed, so callers do not have to infer which condition a hand-written boolean represented.

lessons.title: Reuse constraints with Annotated
lessons.body:
# Reuse constraints with Annotated

Repeating the same bounds on several models makes it easy for their rules to drift. Annotated attaches reusable validation metadata to a type. The resulting alias still communicates its underlying Python type to a type checker, while Pydantic reads the additional constraints at runtime.

Put the alias on collection elements when every element has the rule. A constraint on the collection itself has a different meaning, such as minimum list length. Naming these types also gives an API schema a useful vocabulary.

```python
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import Field, TypeAdapter
Positive = Annotated[int, Field(gt=0)]
values = TypeAdapter(list[Positive])
print(values.validate_python(["2", 3]))
```

Annotated describes each integer, so the list adapter checks every element. An empty collection satisfies an element constraint because it contains no invalid elements.
lessons.explanation: Annotated describes each integer, so the list adapter checks every element. An empty collection satisfies an element constraint because it contains no invalid elements.

lessons.title: Read structured validation errors
lessons.body:
# Read structured validation errors

A validation error can describe several failures at once. Parse its structured `errors()` result instead of scraping the formatted message. Each entry includes a location, a machine-readable error type and a human message.

Locations are tuples and can include collection indexes, so a nested error can identify exactly which item failed. Error messages and documentation URLs may change between versions. Base program logic on locations and error types, and choose deliberately whether raw rejected input belongs in a log or user response.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic import ValidationError
class Row(BaseModel):
    age: int
try:
    Row(age="wrong")
except ValidationError as error:
    print([e["loc"] for e in error.errors()])
```
lessons.task: Implement invalid_fields(raw) validating Profile(name: str, age: int). Return a sorted list of the first location components of all errors, or [] on success. Report both fields when both are absent.
hints: Catch ValidationError from Profile.model_validate(raw).
Read each entry's loc tuple from errors(); collect and sort the first component.
ValidationError.errors returns data, not a display contract. Collecting the first location component is a deliberate summary for this flat model; nested forms should preserve the whole location.
lessons.explanation: ValidationError.errors returns data, not a display contract. Collecting the first location component is a deliberate summary for this flat model; nested forms should preserve the whole location.

lessons.title: Distinguish missing from nullable
lessons.body:
# Distinguish missing from nullable

A nullable field is allowed to contain None. That does not automatically give the field a default. In Pydantic 2, an annotation such as `str | None` is still required unless a default is supplied.

This distinction matters for partial forms and API updates. Missing means the caller did not send a value; an explicit null may mean clear an existing value. Use `model_fields_set` when that distinction must survive validation, and avoid replacing all missing fields with None before you validate them.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
class Note(BaseModel):
    text: str | None = None
print(Note().model_fields_set)
print(Note(text=None).model_fields_set)
```
lessons.task: Define Patch with nullable title defaulting to None. patch_data(raw) must return only fields explicitly supplied, using exclude_unset=True. Preserve an explicit title=None and ignore unknown fields.
hints: A nullable field with default None can still distinguish omission from explicit null.
Dump with exclude_unset=True, which uses model_fields_set rather than comparing values to defaults.
exclude_unset consults which fields were supplied, not whether their values equal the defaults. exclude_none would incorrectly erase an explicit request to clear the title.
lessons.explanation: exclude_unset consults which fields were supplied, not whether their values equal the defaults. exclude_none would incorrectly erase an explicit request to clear the title.

lessons.title: Create independent default containers
lessons.body:
# Create independent default containers

A default value and a default factory express different intentions. A factory is called when an input omits the field, so it can produce a new container or a value computed at construction time. It also makes ownership of mutable state visible to a reader.

Pydantic protects many mutable defaults by copying them, but an explicit factory is clearer when fresh state is part of the contract. Supplied values still go through validation; the factory is not a general hook for transforming every input.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
class Bag(BaseModel):
    tags: list[str] = Field(
        default_factory=list)
a, b = Bag(), Bag()
a.tags.append("new")
print(a.tags, b.tags)
```
lessons.task: Implement independent_tags() constructing two Bag models with tags default_factory=list. Append "new" to the first and return their dumped dictionaries. Neither call may share accumulated state with another call.
hints: Use Field(default_factory=list) on Bag.tags.
Construct two models inside each call, append only to the first, then dump both.
default_factory=list states that each omitted collection starts fresh. Returning ordinary dictionaries also lets a caller inspect the results without retaining model instances.
lessons.explanation: default_factory=list states that each omitted collection starts fresh. Returning ordinary dictionaries also lets a caller inspect the results without retaining model instances.

lessons.title: Reject unknown keys at a boundary
lessons.body:
# Reject unknown keys at a boundary

Pydantic models ignore extra keys by default. That is useful for tolerant readers, but a typo in configuration can then disappear silently. A boundary that owns a fixed vocabulary can reject unknown keys with `extra="forbid"`.

Choose the policy per model. A public response consumer may deliberately tolerate new fields, while a configuration editor should usually report misspellings. Rejecting extras also prevents callers from assuming that arbitrary input fields have been validated merely because the model accepted the rest of the object.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
from pydantic import ValidationError
class Options(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")
    limit: int
try:
    Options(limit=2, limti=3)
except ValidationError as error:
    print(error.errors()[0]["loc"])
```
lessons.task: Define Options with extra="forbid", host: str and port: int default 8000. options_data(raw) returns its validated dictionary and rejects misspelled or unknown keys.

checks.name: rejects unknown keys

hints: Use ConfigDict(extra="forbid") to turn unknown keys into errors.
Declare port with default 8000 and return the validated model's dictionary.
ConfigDict(extra="forbid") makes an unknown key a validation error. The default port applies only when the input omits that declared field.
lessons.explanation: ConfigDict(extra="forbid") makes an unknown key a validation error. The default port applies only when the input omits that declared field.

lessons.title: Validate nested collections
lessons.body:
# Validate nested collections

A boundary often contains a collection of structured records. Nesting models lets Pydantic validate both the outer object and every inner item, while error locations retain the path through the collection.

After validation, the inner values are model instances rather than unchecked dictionaries. Business logic can therefore use attributes and trust the declared constraints. Dumping the outer model recursively serializes those inner models. The input data remains the caller's object; avoid using it as a second, unvalidated source for later calculations.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
class Item(BaseModel):
    units: int
class Order(BaseModel):
    items: list[Item]
order = Order(items=[{"units": "3"}])
print(order.items[0].units)
```
lessons.task: Implement order_total(raw) validating Order(items: list[Line]), where Line has price: float >=0 and quantity: int >0. Return the sum of price times quantity; an empty order costs zero.

checks.name: nested rules apply

hints: Create a Line model and use list[Line] inside Order.
Validate the outer order before summing item.price times item.quantity from typed child instances.
The calculation uses validated Line instances. Constraints on a child model are applied for each item, so one bad quantity invalidates the whole order instead of quietly changing the total.
lessons.explanation: The calculation uses validated Line instances. Constraints on a child model are applied for each item, so one bad quantity invalidates the whole order instead of quietly changing the total.

lessons.title: Separate input names from output names
lessons.body:
# Separate input names from output names

External data does not always use Python's naming style. An alias maps an external key to a model field without forcing that spelling throughout the program. Validation aliases control reading, while serialization aliases control writing.

AliasChoices is useful during a small, explicit migration: accept either the old or the new input key, then emit one canonical name. Choose precedence deliberately if both appear. Dumping by alias is an explicit operation; ordinary dumps use the Python field names unless configured otherwise.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from pydantic import AliasChoices
class User(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(validation_alias=
        AliasChoices("name", "displayName"))
print(User(displayName="Ada").name)
```
lessons.task: Implement canonical_user(raw): accept either user_id or userId as the integer identifier (user_id wins when both occur). Return {"user_id": id}, and reject a missing or invalid identifier.

checks.name: requires a valid identifier

hints: Use Field(validation_alias=AliasChoices("user_id","userId")).
The first alias wins; an ordinary model_dump returns the Python field name user_id.
AliasChoices lists accepted input keys in priority order. model_dump returns the canonical Python field name, so downstream code does not have to handle several spellings.
lessons.explanation: AliasChoices lists accepted input keys in priority order. model_dump returns the canonical Python field name, so downstream code does not have to handle several spellings.

lessons.title: Check relationships between fields
lessons.body:
# Check relationships between fields

Some rules involve more than one field. A valid start and a valid end do not necessarily form a valid interval. An after model validator sees the parsed model and can enforce that relationship in one place.

Return the instance after checking it. The validator should express a domain invariant rather than repair arbitrary contradictory data. Field errors are still reported by the fields themselves; the model-level rule is reached only after those fields have been parsed successfully. Equality at a boundary remains a separate policy decision.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic import model_validator
class Span(BaseModel):
    start: int
    end: int
    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def ordered(self):
        if self.end < self.start:
            raise ValueError("reversed span")
        return self
print(Span(start=2, end=5).end)
```
lessons.task: Implement span_length(raw) with Span(start: int, end: int). Validate end >= start using a model validator, and return end-start. A zero-length interval is valid.

checks.name: rejects reversed intervals

hints: Use model_validator(mode="after") to compare two parsed fields.
Reject end less than start, return self, then compute end minus start in the function.
The model validator checks a relationship on typed fields and returns self. Inclusive ordering allows equality, which is why length zero is a valid result.
lessons.explanation: The model validator checks a relationship on typed fields and returns self. Inclusive ordering allows equality, which is why length zero is a valid result.

lessons.title: Select a model with a discriminator
lessons.body:
# Select a model with a discriminator

An untagged union may try several candidate models before deciding what the input means. A discriminator makes the decision explicit: a literal tag selects one branch, and only that branch's fields are validated.

This works well for events, commands and configuration variants. Give each branch a unique tag and preserve it when serializing. An unknown tag is an error, not a reason to guess a branch. Fields valid for a different variant must not accidentally make an invalid event appear acceptable.

```python
from typing import Annotated, Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from pydantic import TypeAdapter
class Add(BaseModel):
    kind: Literal["add"]
    amount: int
Event = Annotated[Add, Field()]
print(TypeAdapter(Event).validate_python(
    {"kind": "add", "amount": "3"}))
```
lessons.task: Implement event_value(raw) validating a discriminated union: Add(kind="add", amount:int) or Remove(kind="remove", key:str). Return the amount or key. Reject unknown tags and missing branch fields.
lessons.solution:
from typing import Annotated, Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, TypeAdapter
class Add(BaseModel):
    kind: Literal['add']
    amount: int
class Remove(BaseModel):
    kind: Literal['remove']
    key: str
Event = Annotated[Add | Remove, Field(discriminator='kind')]
def event_value(raw):
    item=TypeAdapter(Event).validate_python(raw)
    return item.amount if isinstance(item,Add) else item.key

checks.name: rejects invalid variants

hints: Give each branch a Literal kind and set Field(discriminator="kind") on their Annotated union.
Validate with TypeAdapter, then inspect the concrete Add or Remove instance to choose its value.
The kind field selects exactly one model. After validation the result is a concrete Add or Remove instance, so ordinary isinstance dispatch is unambiguous.
lessons.explanation: The kind field selects exactly one model. After validation the result is a concrete Add or Remove instance, so ordinary isinstance dispatch is unambiguous.

lessons.title: Validate a type without a wrapper model
lessons.body:
# Validate a type without a wrapper model

Not every boundary is a named record. A JSON endpoint might return a list of integers or a mapping of names to counts. TypeAdapter validates those existing Python type expressions without inventing an artificial BaseModel field around them.

Create an adapter once when repeatedly validating the same type. It can validate Python objects or JSON text, and can also serialize values. Validation of raw JSON and serialization of an already trusted value are different operations; do not assume dumping a bad value performs validation first.

```python
from pydantic import TypeAdapter
adapter = TypeAdapter(dict[str, int])
print(adapter.validate_json(
    '{"tea": "2", "water": 1}'))
```
lessons.task: Implement parse_counts(text) using TypeAdapter(dict[str,int]).validate_json. Return a dictionary of integer counts. Reject malformed JSON, nonobject JSON and values that cannot become integers.

checks.name: rejects invalid JSON or shape

hints: TypeAdapter can validate dict[str,int] directly without a BaseModel wrapper.
Use validate_json on the text so malformed JSON and invalid dictionary values are both rejected.
TypeAdapter expresses the actual top-level type. validate_json combines JSON decoding and validation, preserving one consistent error interface for both malformed text and invalid values.
lessons.explanation: TypeAdapter expresses the actual top-level type. validate_json combines JSON decoding and validation, preserving one consistent error interface for both malformed text and invalid values.

lessons.title: Give a root collection model behaviour
lessons.body:
# Give a root collection model behaviour

A RootModel wraps one value at the root instead of declaring an object with several named fields. Its root may be a list, a dictionary or another supported type. Unlike an ordinary model with a field called root, its JSON representation is the root value itself.

Use it when a collection deserves a model's validation methods or additional behaviour but the external format must remain a bare collection. Access the parsed collection through `.root`. Choose TypeAdapter instead if you only need validation and no named model behaviour.

```python
from pydantic import RootModel
class Tags(RootModel[list[str]]):
    pass
tags = Tags.model_validate(["tea", "new"])
print(tags.root)
print(tags.model_dump_json())
```
lessons.task: Implement root_numbers(raw) with a RootModel[list[int]]. Return (the sum of .root, the dumped collection). Empty input returns (0, []). Reject an invalid member.

checks.name: validates members

hints: Subclass RootModel[list[int]], then call model_validate on the incoming collection.
Read numbers from .root; model_dump returns the bare collection rather than a dictionary containing root.
RootModel serializes the collection directly rather than adding a root key. The .root attribute supplies the validated values for model behaviour such as aggregation.
lessons.explanation: RootModel serializes the collection directly rather than adding a root key. The .root attribute supplies the validated values for model behaviour such as aggregation.

lessons.title: Serialize Python values for JSON
lessons.body:
# Serialize Python values for JSON

A model can contain values that JSON has no native representation for, such as dates, UUIDs or sets. A normal Python dump preserves many of those useful Python objects. A JSON-mode dump converts them to a representation JSON can encode.

Choose the format at the boundary where it is needed. Keep date objects for calculations and produce text when writing a response or file. `model_dump_json()` returns JSON text, while `model_dump(mode="json")` returns JSON-compatible Python data. These are different return contracts even when they represent the same information.

```python
from datetime import date
from pydantic import BaseModel
class Event(BaseModel):
    day: date
item = Event(day="2026-01-02")
print(type(item.model_dump()["day"]).__name__)
print(item.model_dump(mode="json"))
```

JSON mode converts the validated date to ISO text while retaining the dictionary shape. The model validates calendar dates before serialization, so formatting cannot conceal an impossible date.
lessons.explanation: JSON mode converts the validated date to ISO text while retaining the dictionary shape. The model validates calendar dates before serialization, so formatting cannot conceal an impossible date.

lessons.title: Expose derived data with computed_field
lessons.body:
# Expose derived data with computed_field

Derived data should have one source of truth. Storing a subtotal alongside its inputs allows the values to disagree. A computed field exposes a property in model serialization while calculating its value from validated inputs.

The property is not an independently validated input field. Use it for deterministic derived information, and remember that repeatedly accessing an ordinary property recomputes it. Keep expensive or effectful work out of serialization. If a value depends on external state, computing it explicitly in a service is usually a clearer boundary.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic import computed_field
class Square(BaseModel):
    side: int
    @computed_field
    @property
    def area(self) -> int:
        return self.side * self.side
print(Square(side=3).model_dump())
```

lessons.explanation: computed_field includes the typed property in serialization. Because total is derived from validated price and quantity, a conflicting extra input cannot replace the calculation.

lessons.title: Keep invariants when fields change
lessons.body:
# Keep invariants when fields change

Validation at construction does not automatically validate every later assignment. A model that begins valid can otherwise be changed into an invalid state. Enable assignment validation when a mutable model must preserve its field rules after construction.

Another choice is a frozen model and explicit reconstruction. Neither choice makes nested mutable containers deeply immutable. Also, `model_copy(update=...)` is a trusted-data operation, not a general replacement for validating untrusted updates. Select the update boundary deliberately and test that rejected updates leave the previous value intact.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
from pydantic import Field, ValidationError
class Counter(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(
        validate_assignment=True)
    count: int = Field(ge=0)
item = Counter(count=2)
try:
    item.count = -1
except ValidationError:
    print(item.count)
```
lessons.task: Implement update_count(initial,new) using a Counter model with count>=0 and validate_assignment=True. Return (accepted, final_count), catching a rejected assignment but allowing invalid initial construction to raise.

checks.name: initial construction is validated

hints: Set validate_assignment=True and Field(ge=0) on count.
Construct first, then catch ValidationError only around the assignment so invalid initial values still raise.
Assignment validation applies the field schema on every write. A failed field assignment leaves the previous value in place, which is different from mutating an unchecked dictionary.
lessons.explanation: Assignment validation applies the field schema on every write. A failed field assignment leaves the previous value in place, which is different from mutating an unchecked dictionary.

lessons.title: Derive a schema from the validated model
lessons.body:
# Derive a schema from the validated model

A schema describes a data contract in a machine-readable form. Deriving it from the same model used for validation reduces the chance that documentation and actual input rules disagree. JSON Schema includes types, required fields and constraints; it is not itself a successful validation of any particular input.

Inspect the part of the schema your integration needs instead of comparing an entire generated document byte for byte. Titles and definition ordering are presentation details. Optional fields with defaults and required fields also need different treatment in forms and client generators.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
class Query(BaseModel):
    limit: int = Field(ge=1, le=50)
schema = Query.model_json_schema()
print(schema["required"])
print(schema["properties"]["limit"]["minimum"])
```
lessons.task: Implement query_schema() from a Query model: required term:str of length>=1, limit:int default10 in 1..100. Return its JSON Schema. Use model_json_schema instead of hand-writing a separate contract.
hints: Declare constraints on the real Query model.
Return Query.model_json_schema(); a defaulted limit is not a required field.
The generated schema and the model share one declaration. Tests inspect meaningful constraints rather than generated titles or key ordering, making the contract both explicit and stable.
lessons.explanation: The generated schema and the model share one declaration. Tests inspect meaningful constraints rather than generated titles or key ordering, making the contract both explicit and stable.
